title: DoorDash's Flux Runs 130,000 Engineering Tasks Through Cloud-Based Agents
gist: DoorDash built Flux, an internal cloud-based agentic engineering platform using Firecracker microVM sandboxes and an in-house MCP gateway, moving coding-agent workloads off developer laptops; it automated 130,000 engineering tasks and 25,000+ code reviews weekly in a single month in 2026, illustrating a broader industry shift toward centralized, governed cloud execution for AI coding agents (also seen at GitHub Copilot).

themes.theme: Scale and adoption metrics of Flux

insights.claim: DoorDash's Flux cloud platform automated 130,000 engineering tasks in a single month in 2026, supports more than 25,000 automated code reviews per week, and runs more than 300 playbooks with over 10,000 weekly invocations, allowing workflows to run unattended and in parallel.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: These are concrete, large-scale production usage numbers for an enterprise agentic-engineering platform — a benchmark investors can use to gauge how far internal AI-agent tooling has scaled at a major tech employer, and a comparison point for competing platforms (GitHub Copilot, internal tools at peers).
insights.quote: DoorDash has moved engineering agent workloads from developers’ laptops to its Flux cloud platform, which automated 130,000 engineering tasks in a single month in 2026.

insights.claim: DoorDash initially deployed Flux for automated code review, described internally as a frequent and measurable workflow, then expanded it to CI triage, on-call tasks, maintenance workflows, and ticket-driven development.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: The land-and-expand rollout pattern (start with a measurable, low-risk workflow, then broaden scope) is a reusable adoption playbook for enterprises introducing agentic engineering tools internally.
insights.quote: DoorDash initially used Flux for automated code review, which the company described as a frequent and measurable workflow.

themes.theme: Why DoorDash moved off laptop-based agents

insights.claim: DoorDash built Flux after encountering concrete limitations with agent workloads running on individual developer laptops: local execution limits available CPU and memory, depends on the developer's device staying connected, and gives autonomous agents access to credentials and internal systems already available to that developer.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Articulates a specific, generalizable causal case against laptop-based coding-agent deployment for security and reliability reasons — relevant to any enterprise weighing local versus cloud-sandboxed agent execution, a decision point that favors vendors offering managed sandbox infrastructure.
insights.quote: Local execution limits available CPU and memory, depends on the developer’s device remaining connected, and can give autonomous agents access to credentials and internal systems already available to the developer.

insights.claim: DoorDash found local agent execution also makes it harder to monitor where agents are running, which systems they access, and on whose behalf they operate.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Observability and auditability gaps in laptop-based agent execution are a direct driver of enterprise demand for centralized agent platforms and gateways — a market opportunity for security/observability vendors serving AI-agent workloads.
insights.quote: DoorDash also said local execution makes it harder to monitor where agents are running, which systems they access, and on whose behalf they operate.

insights.claim: Radoslav Krehlik, DoorDash's security architect, said Flux was built after laptop-based agents ran into limits on power, uptime, and security, and that engineers can trigger agents from Slack, GitHub, or scheduled jobs while DoorDash retains full enterprise security guardrails.
insights.speaker: Radoslav Krehlik
insights.so_what: Direct practitioner confirmation from DoorDash's own security architect that centralized, guardrailed agent execution is now viewed as the necessary model for enterprise-scale agentic engineering, not merely an efficiency nicety.
insights.quote: Built after laptop-based agents ran into limits on power, uptime, and security. Engineers can trigger the agents from Slack, GitHub, or scheduled jobs while DoorDash keeps full enterprise security guardrails

insights.claim: Flux is built around four platform primitives: cloud sandboxes for isolated execution, an MCP gateway controlling access to internal systems, reusable playbooks defining the work, and invocation surfaces (Slack, GitHub, cron, command line, conversational interfaces) that start workflows.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A four-primitive architecture (sandbox/gateway/playbook/invocation) is emerging as a reference pattern for enterprise agentic-engineering platforms — useful for benchmarking competing internal or vendor platforms against a common structure.
insights.quote: Flux is built around four platform primitives: cloud sandboxes, an MCP gateway, reusable playbooks, and invocation surfaces.

insights.claim: Flux's sandboxes use Firecracker micro virtual machines to isolate agent workloads, with each environment provisioned with the repositories, development tools, secrets, and runtime dependencies required for a specific task, and DoorDash reports a 95th-percentile SLO of under five seconds for end-to-end sandbox setup including microVM start, repo cloning, build tool installation, and coding-agent harness configuration.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A sub-five-second p95 SLO for full sandbox provisioning is a strong performance benchmark for Firecracker-based agent sandboxing at scale, useful for comparing against other cloud sandbox providers (e.g., GitHub's cloud coding-agent environments) on cold-start latency.
insights.quote: DoorDash reports a 95th percentile service level objective of less than five seconds for end-to-end sandbox setup, including starting the microVM, cloning repositories, installing build tools, and configuring the coding agent harness.

insights.claim: Agents access DoorDash’s internal systems through Agent Gateway, an in-house MCP gateway providing scoped permissions and logging agent activity for auditing and policy enforcement.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: An in-house MCP gateway for permission-scoping and audit logging is becoming standard enterprise infrastructure for agent-to-internal-system access, a functional category third-party vendors (API gateway, identity, and observability companies) can target.
insights.quote: Agents access DoorDash’s internal systems through Agent Gateway, an in-house MCP gateway that provides scoped permissions and logs agent activity for auditing and policy enforcement.

insights.claim: Playbooks are defined in YAML and specify the task, required tools, permissions, validation, and safety boundaries, and can combine agent-driven steps with deterministic code where predictable execution or validation is required.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Mixing deterministic code with agent-driven steps inside a declarative playbook format is a practical risk-mitigation pattern for production agentic workflows, relevant to any platform team designing similar internal tooling.
insights.quote: Playbooks, defined in YAML, specify the task, required tools, permissions, validation, and safety boundaries. They can combine agent-driven steps with deterministic code where predictable execution or validation is required.

themes.theme: Industry trend toward cloud-based agent execution

insights.claim: Duy Nguyễn, Co-founder of TOP GROUP Vietnam, argues that once agents handle background work, code review, internal tools, and concurrent execution, the hard problem shifts from model choice to control: identity, permissions, sandboxing, audit logs, quotas, and a real kill switch.
insights.speaker: Duy Nguyễn
insights.so_what: A concise thesis that the competitive and investment frontier in agentic engineering is shifting from model capability to control-plane infrastructure (identity, permissions, audit, kill switches) — favoring infra/security vendors over pure model providers as agent adoption scales.
insights.quote: Once agents handle background work, code review, internal tools, and concurrent execution, the hard problem shifts from model choice to control: identity, permissions, sandboxing, audit logs, quotas, and a real kill switch.

insights.claim: DoorDash's move to cloud-based agent execution is part of a broader industry shift; GitHub supports both local and cloud sandbox environments for Copilot with controls over filesystem, network, and system access, and its cloud sandboxes let agents execute coding tasks without consuming local developer resources.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: GitHub Copilot offering comparable cloud sandbox execution confirms this is a converging industry pattern rather than a DoorDash-specific choice, suggesting cloud agent sandboxing is becoming table-stakes infrastructure across coding-agent vendors.
insights.quote: GitHub supports both local and cloud sandbox environments for Copilot, with controls over filesystem, network, and system access.
insights.locator: paragraph on broader move toward cloud-based execution

insights.claim: DoorDash changed its Slack integration for Flux from private channels to public threads so engineers could observe agent executions, review results, and see how other teams delegated work to agents.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A small but telling organizational design choice: making agent activity socially visible (public threads) to build trust and cross-team learning is a low-cost adoption-acceleration tactic other enterprises rolling out internal agent platforms could replicate.
insights.quote: DoorDash also changed its Slack integration from private channels to public threads so engineers could observe agent executions, review results, and see how other teams delegated work.
